summary: Lists architectural and functional requirements for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance in the MPLS Transport Profile. They apply to pseudowires, label switched paths and sections. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It lists the tools a repair crew needs to check, watch and fix a train line.

questions: what are oam requirements for mpls transport
what is fate sharing in oam
subtitle: The checklist of health-check and troubleshooting tools that MPLS transport networks must be able to offer.

tldr.problem: Transport network operators need to watch their paths, find faults and verify service levels, and the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) needed an agreed list of what its OAM tools must do.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists architectural requirements (in-band, independent of IP, configurable without a control plane) and twelve groups of functional requirements such as continuity checks, route tracing, lock, alarm reporting and loss and delay measurement. It leaves the protocols that meet them to other documents.
tldr.outcome: The protocol designers had a shared target for MPLS-TP OAM. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no replacement.

today: RFC 5860 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states requirements only; the protocols that meet them are defined in other documents.

sections.title: Why Transport Networks Need OAM
sections.content:
OAM stands for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance. In the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) it serves two purposes. It is a network-oriented tool, used by an operator to monitor the infrastructure and to trigger things like protection when a node or link fails. It is also a service-oriented tool, used by a service provider to watch the services sold to customers and to verify some Service Level Agreement (SLA) parameters.

The RFC says OAM helps reduce operational complexity and cost, improves network availability by finding faults before a customer reports them, and helps meet service and performance objectives, for example by detecting degradation due to packet delay or loss.

The requirements apply to pseudowires (PWs), Label Switched Paths (LSPs) and Sections. They are derived from requirements published by ITU-T in Y.Sup4 and complement RFC 4377. The document lists requirements only. It does not say how protocols should behave, and it does not say which function to use for which application.

The RFC defines a few working terms. A fault is the inability of a function to perform a required action. A defect is a density of anomalies high enough to interrupt a required function. Proactive OAM runs continuously or over long periods, while on-demand OAM is started manually for a limited time to troubleshoot. An End Point is an LER (for an LSP or Section) or a T-PE (for a PW); an Intermediate Point is an LSR or an S-PE.
sections.eli5: Network owners want to know when a path breaks before customers complain. OAM is the set of check-up tools that does that, like a doctor's kit for the network.

sections.title: Architectural Requirements
sections.content:
The architectural requirements describe the shape any OAM solution must have.

  • Scope. Solutions MUST at least apply to point-to-point bidirectional PWs, point-to-point co-routed bidirectional LSPs and point-to-point bidirectional Sections. They MUST work end-to-end and on segments, across multiple domains, and on any LSP regardless of label stack depth.
  • Independence. Solutions SHOULD be independent of the underlying tunneling or transmission technology and of the service a PW emulates. OAM on a segment SHOULD be independent of OAM on the end-to-end path, and it SHOULD be possible to tell their packets apart.
  • Data plane. OAM packets MUST run in-band, following the exact same path as user traffic. This is often called fate sharing. It MUST be possible to tell OAM packets from user traffic.
  • IP optional. OAM MUST be deployable where IP capabilities exist and where they may not. It MUST be possible to operate OAM with or without relying on IP. Identification information MUST at least support an IP addressing structure and be extensible to other schemes.
  • Interworking. When MPLS-TP runs with IP routing and forwarding, existing IP/MPLS and PW OAM protocols such as LSP-Ping, MPLS-BFD, VCCV and VCCV-BFD MUST still be usable.
  • Configuration. OAM MUST operate and be configurable even without a control plane. Enabling or disabling OAM on an established connection MUST NOT make the customer perceive service degradation.
sections.eli5: The inspection car has to ride on the same track as the passenger trains, so it finds the same problems. And it has to work even if the track has no fancy signalling system.

sections.title: Functional Requirements: Checking the Path
sections.content:
The functional requirements form the MPLS-TP OAM toolset. The list may not be exhaustive, so mechanisms SHALL be extensible, and experimental OAM functions MUST be possible but disabled by default. Using any OAM function MUST be optional, and unless stated otherwise functions MUST NOT rely on user traffic.

Four functions check that a path exists and where it goes:

  • Continuity checks let an End Point monitor the liveness of a PW, LSP or Section. They SHOULD be proactive.
  • Connectivity verification lets an End Point determine whether it is connected to the specific End Point(s) it expects, over the expected path. It SHOULD be proactive between End Points and on-demand between End Points and Intermediate Points.
  • Route tracing discovers the Intermediate and End Points along the path, and the information collected MUST include identifiers of nodes and interfaces. It SHOULD be on-demand.
  • Diagnostic tests include, as examples, a loop-back at a node that returns all OAM and data traffic to the originating End Point, and estimating the bandwidth of an LSP. They SHOULD be on-demand.

The RFC also says that on-demand functions whose result may vary with packet size SHOULD be usable with different packet sizes.
sections.eli5: These tools answer simple questions: is the track alive, does it really go where we expect, which stations does it pass, and does it work if we send a test train round the loop?

sections.title: Locks, Alarms and Failure Reports
sections.content:
A general requirement comes first: if a defect or fault occurs on a PW, LSP or Section, mechanisms MUST detect, diagnose, localize and notify the appropriate nodes. A service provider MUST be able to learn of a fault affecting its service even when the fault is outside its own domain.

Several functions then carry state and fault information between nodes.

  • Lock instruct: an End Point tells its peer End Point(s) to lock the path. Lock is an administrative status in which only test traffic, if any, and the path's own OAM are expected on it. It SHOULD be on-demand.
  • Lock reporting: an Intermediate Point reports to an End Point a lock on a tunnel LSP that indirectly affects the PW or LSP. It SHOULD be proactive.
  • Alarm reporting: the same idea for a fault or defect on a tunnel LSP. It SHOULD be proactive.
  • Remote defect indication: an End Point tells its associated End Point about a fault or defect it detects. It SHOULD be proactive.
  • Client failure indication: carries information about a client-side defect from edge to edge of the MPLS-TP network, if the client layer OAM does not provide alarm propagation. It SHOULD be proactive.
sections.eli5: When one part of the track is closed or broken, these messages tell the station staff at both ends, so nobody keeps sending trains into the problem.

sections.title: Measuring Packet Loss and Delay
sections.content:
Packet loss measurement MUST quantify the packet loss ratio over a PW, LSP or Section. The RFC defines the ratio as the number of user packets lost divided by the total number of user packets sent during a defined time interval, and takes the definition of a lost packet from RFC 2680. It MAY be proactive or on-demand, and it SHOULD be possible to rely on user traffic to perform it.

Packet delay measurement MUST quantify the one-way and, if appropriate, the two-way delay. One-way delay (from RFC 2679) runs from the start of transmission of a packet's first bit by one End Point to the reception of its last bit by the other End Point. Two-way delay (from RFC 2681) is measured from the same start until the last bit is received back at the same End Point, and may use a data traffic loopback at the remote End Point. Accurate one-way delay may require clock synchronization, which is out of scope. Delay measurement SHOULD be on-demand and MAY be proactive.

For point-to-point associated bidirectional LSPs, unidirectional LSPs and point-to-multipoint LSPs, delay measurement is only required to quantify one-way delay.
sections.eli5: These tools count how many trains went missing and how long a trip takes. That lets the railway prove it kept its promises to customers.

sections.title: Congestion and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Section 3 asks for one mechanism, such as rate limiting, to prevent OAM packets from causing congestion in the packet switched network.

On security, the RFC says it does not itself imply any security consideration, but OAM does. OAM messages can reveal sensitive information such as passwords, performance data and details of the network topology, so some form of authentication, authorization and encryption is suggested. Management stations SHOULD be designed so OAM functions cannot be accessed without authorization.

OAM protocol solutions MUST let messages be authenticated to prove their origin and to make sure they are destined for the receiving node, and the use of that facility MUST be configurable. An OAM packet received over a PW, LSP or Section MUST NOT be forwarded beyond the End Point, so that it does not leave the current administrative domain.
sections.eli5: Inspection messages can contain secrets about the railway, so they need a lock, and they must never leave the railway's own property. Also, inspectors must not send so many messages that they cause a traffic jam.
